questions.prompt: Expand (1−4x)^(1/2) to the x² term and state the convergence interval. [4 marks]
questions.modelAnswer: Use 1+nu+[n(n−1)/2]u² with n=1/2 and u=−4x. Linear coefficient is (1/2)(−4x)=−2x. Quadratic term is [(1/2)(−1/2)/2]×16x²=−2x². The series is 1−2x−2x²+… for |x|<1/4.

questions.prompt: For small nonzero x in radians, find the limiting value of [sin(4x)+2x]/sin(3x) as x→0. [3 marks]
markPoints: For small angles in radians, sin(4x)≈4x and sin(3x)≈3x.
questions.modelAnswer: For small angles in radians, sin(4x)≈4x and sin(3x)≈3x. The numerator is approximately 4x+2x=6x. The ratio tends to 6x/(3x)=2.

questions.prompt: The curve x²y+y³=10 goes through (1,2). Find the gradient and the normal at this point. [5 marks]

questions.prompt: For f(x)=(x−1)²+2 with x≥1, find its range, inverse and the range of g(f(x)) if g(t)=√t. [5 marks]
markPoints: Complete square form shows the minimum of f is 2 at x=1; range f≥2.
From y=(x−1)²+2 and x≥1, take x=1+√(y−2).
Since f≥2 and square root is increasing, its range is y≥√2.
questions.modelAnswer: Complete square form shows the minimum of f is 2 at x=1; range f≥2. From y=(x−1)²+2 and x≥1, take x=1+√(y−2). Therefore f⁻¹(x)=1+√(x−2), for x≥2. The composition is g(f(x))=√((x−1)²+2). Since f≥2 and square root is increasing, its range is y≥√2.

questions.prompt: Solve sin(x+π/6)=cos x for 0≤x<2π. [5 marks]
markPoints: The alternative sine branch gives π/6=π/2+2kπ, impossible for integer k.
Solutions in range are x=π/6 and x=7π/6.
questions.modelAnswer: Rewrite cos x as sin(π/2−x). One sine branch is x+π/6=π/2−x+2kπ. Hence x=π/6+kπ. The alternative sine branch gives π/6=π/2+2kπ, impossible for integer k. Solutions in range are x=π/6 and x=7π/6.

questions.prompt: Solve (x+1)/(x−2)>0, explaining the critical values and the excluded point. [4 marks]
markPoints: The numerator vanishes at x=−1 and the denominator at x=2.
Exclude x=2; also exclude x=−1 because the inequality is strict.
The ratio is positive when numerator and denominator share sign.
questions.modelAnswer: The numerator vanishes at x=−1 and the denominator at x=2. Exclude x=2; also exclude x=−1 because the inequality is strict. The ratio is positive when numerator and denominator share sign. Solution: x<−1 or x>2.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: New original Year 13 Pure exam-method practice
questions.prompt: The cubic f(x)=x³+ax²+bx+1 has stationary points at x=1 and x=3. Find a,b and the nature of both points. [5 marks]
markPoints: Equate coefficients to obtain a=−6 and b=9.
At x=1 f″=−6, a local maximum; at x=3 f″=6, a local minimum.
questions.modelAnswer: The derivative f′(x)=3x²+2ax+b. Its roots 1 and 3 imply f′(x)=3(x−1)(x−3)=3x²−12x+9. Equate coefficients to obtain a=−6 and b=9. The second derivative is f″(x)=6x−12. At x=1 f″=−6, a local maximum; at x=3 f″=6, a local minimum.

questions.subject: Maths
questions.series: New original Year 13 Pure exam-method practice
questions.prompt: For y=x³ln x on x>0, find the stationary point and decide if it is a maximum or minimum. [5 marks]
markPoints: Differentiate using product rule: y′=x²(3ln x+1).
Set y′=0 to get ln x=−1/3 and x=e^(−1/3).
At the stationary point y″=x(−2+5)>0, so it is a local minimum.
questions.modelAnswer: Differentiate using product rule: y′=x²(3ln x+1). Set y′=0 to get ln x=−1/3 and x=e^(−1/3). At that x, y=(e^−1)(−1/3)=−1/(3e). Differentiate again: y″=x(6ln x+5). At the stationary point y″=x(−2+5)>0, so it is a local minimum.

questions.prompt: Prove by contradiction: if xy is irrational for real x,y, at least one of x,y is irrational. [4 marks]

This contradicts xy being irrational; therefore at least one factor is irrational.
